overview.description: Pelmanism (known globally as Concentration, Memory, or Shinkei-suijaku in Japan) is the definitive card game for testing visualization and spatial memory. Played with a standard 52-card deck spread face-down, players take turns flipping two cards to find matches. It is a universal game played by all ages, from toddlers to memory champions, and serves as the foundation for countless themed 'Memory' games.

history.origins: Named after the 'Pelman Institute', a London-based school founded in 1899 that focused on 'mind training' and mnemonics.
timeline: 1900s: The Pelman Institute popularizes 'Memory' exercises which evolve into the game.
1950s: Modern themed 'Memory' card sets (like Ravensburger) are mass-produced.
1980s: Digital versions appear on early computerized toys and PCs.
Present: A cornerstone of early childhood education and cognitive therapy.
history.evolution: In Japan, the game is called 'Shinkei-suijaku' (Nervous Breakdown), reflecting the mental strain of tracking 52 cards.
history.cultural: Used as the baseline for many cognitive psychology experiments regarding short-term and working memory.

setup.players: 2 is standard; it also works as a solitaire challenge.
setup.deck: 52 cards (or any deck with an even number of cards).
setup.dealing: All cards are laid out face-down in a grid (usually 4x13 or similar) or scattered randomly on the table.

rules.objective: Players take turns turning face up two cards from the face-down layout; when the two cards match by rank (suits ignored), the player takes the pair and takes another turn. The player who has collected the most pairs when all cards have been taken wins.
rules.gameplay: Lay cards face-down. Turn over two at a time. Match pairs: same rank (suits ignored). If they match, take the pair and take another turn; if not, turn them face down and pass the turn. Most pairs wins.
keyRules: Match is same rank (denomination); suits are ignored. If the two turned cards match, take the pair to your pile and take another turn. If they do not match, turn them face down in place and the turn passes to the next player.

strategy.basic: Don't flip cards at random! Watch your opponent's turn with total focus. If they flip a Queen and then a 7, memorize those positions. When it's your turn, if you flip a Queen, you should already know exactly where the other Queen is. Even the best players can only track about 10-15 cards at a time; focus on one region of the grid.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Safe First Flip': Always flip a card whose identity you DO NOT know for your first card. If you happen to flip a card that you've seen before, you can then use your second flip to take the matching pair from its known location. Never flip a 'Known' card first unless you have no other choice.
strategy.advanced: Grid-Anchor Technique: Mentally divide the grid into quadrants (Top-Left, Bottom-Right, etc.). Assign high cards to the 'corners' in your mind. If you find a Joker or an Ace, use it as a 'Landmark' to remember the cards around it. Pro players often count the number of cards in each row to create a coordinate system (e.g., 'Row 2, Card 4').
tips: If you are playing with children, use fewer cards (e.g., only use the 1s through 6s).
Pay attention to the 'Flipped Back' cards. The sound of the card hitting the table is a mnemonic trigger for some people.

difficulty.easy: Completely random; forgets locations after 1 turn; misses obvious matches.
difficulty.medium: Remembers up to 6 locations; reliably matches cards seen in the current round.
difficulty.hard: Perfect memory; tracks the coordinates of all 52 cards; only misses if it hasn't seen the cards yet.

edgeCases.text: First player is chosen by agreement; there is no dealer. When all cards are taken as pairs, the player with most pairs wins; ties share the win.

customActions.description: Turn face up two cards from the tableau. If they match by rank, take the pair to your collected pile and take another turn; otherwise turn them face down and pass the turn.
customActions.constraints: Exactly two cards must be chosen from the face-down tableau. Match is same rank; suits are ignored.

engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck comprising four suits: Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, and Spades. Each suit contains thirteen ranks: Ace, 2 through 10, Jack, Queen, and King, providing versatile options for various card games.
engine.suitDescription: Suits and ranks are as defined in the deck description above; no separate suit or rank set is used for this game.
engine.rankDescription: Suits and ranks are as defined in the deck description above; no separate suit or rank set is used for this game.
engine.dealPattern: All cards spread face-down on the table in a regular or irregular layout; no overlap.
